title: Changing items, one or many
idea: Fluency with item assignment, including changing items inside a loop with range(len(...)). Combines assignment, indexing, and len.

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

n = [1, 2, 3]
n[0] = 10
n[2] = 30
print(n)
exercises.explanation: Two assignments: spot 0 becomes 10, spot 2 becomes 30. The middle item is untouched: [10, 2, 30].

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

n = [5, 5, 5]
n[1] = n[1] * 2
print(n)
exercises.explanation: n[1] is 5; 5 * 2 is 10; that goes back into spot 1. Only the middle item changes: [5, 10, 5].

exercises.prompt: You can read an item and write to the same spot in one line, like n[0] = n[0] + 1.
exercises.explanation: The right side is computed first using the old value, then stored back in the spot. It's the list version of count = count + 1.

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

n = [2, 4, 6]
for i in range(len(n)):
    n[i] = n[i] + 1
print(n)
exercises.explanation: For each position i, add 1 to n[i]. 2->3, 4->5, 6->7, giving [3, 5, 7]. The loop changes every item in place.

exercises.prompt:
Double every item. Fill in the position used on both sides:

n = [1, 2, 3]
for i in range(len(n)):
    n[i] = n[____] * 2
print(n)
exercises.explanation: Both sides use position i: n[i] = n[i] * 2. The loop doubles each item, giving [2, 4, 6].

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

n = [7, 8, 9]
for i in range(len(n)):
    n[i] = 0
print(n)
exercises.explanation: Every position is set to 0, so the whole list becomes [0, 0, 0]. Assigning in a loop can reset every item.

exercises.prompt: Arrange code that adds 10 to every item in the list.
exercises.explanation: Loop over every position and add 10 to each item: [11, 12, 13]. range(len(n)) hits every spot.

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

n = [3, 1, 4]
n[1] = 1
print(n)
exercises.explanation: Position 1 already held 1, and we assigned 1 again — no visible change. Assigning the same value is harmless.

exercises.prompt: Why use range(len(n)) when changing every item in a loop?
options: It visits exactly the valid positions, so n[i] is always safe
exercises.explanation: range(len(n)) gives 0 up to len-1 — every real position. So n[i] never goes out of range, whatever the length.

exercises.prompt:
Same code, new list:

n = [0, 0]
for i in range(len(n)):
    n[i] = n[i] + 5
print(n)

What shows?
exercises.explanation: Each 0 gets 5 added, giving [5, 5]. The same 'change every item' loop adapts to the new values and length.
